california: California covers 163,696 square miles and is bordered by Oregon to the north, Nevada to the east, Arizona to the south-east, the Mexican state of Baja California to the south and the Pacific Ocean to the west. In the middle lies the Central Valley, bounded by the Sierra Nevada and the coastal ranges, the state's agricultural heartland. The name most likely comes from the mythical island of California in the 1510 romance The Adventures of Esplandián by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo, whose Queen Calafia ruled a remote land rich in gold and pearls. The name was on a map by 1541. The Spaniards called the peninsula of Baja California Las Californias, and the name spread north to Alta California.

Before European colonisation California was one of the most culturally and linguistically diverse areas of pre-Columbian North America. Historians generally agree that at least 300,000 people lived there, in more than 70 ethnic groups. They managed their environments in complex ways, with forest gardening and controlled burning to prevent destructive wildfires, and political organisation ranged from bands and villages to large chiefdoms on the rich coasts, among them the Chumash, Pomo and Salinan.

European exploration in the 16th and 17th centuries led to colonisation by the Spanish Empire. The area became part of Mexico in 1821. In the Mexican-American War the United States conquered California, and Mexico ceded it in 1848. The gold rush that began that year brought social and demographic changes, among them what has been called the California genocide of the Indigenous peoples. California was admitted as the 31st state in 1850, as a free state, following the Compromise of 1850.

Sacramento is the state capital, and Los Angeles is its most populous city. California is the most populous US state, with over 39 million people. Hollywood has been an important centre of the film industry since the 1920s, and Silicon Valley in the San Francisco Bay Area is a centre of the technology industry.
cambodia: Cambodia covers about 181,035 km2 and lies entirely within the tropics, with a 443 km coastline along the Gulf of Thailand. Its landscape is a low-lying central plain surrounded by uplands and low mountains, including the Tonle Sap, the Great Lake, and the upper Mekong delta. The Tonle Sap's most distinctive feature is its flooding, from about 2,590 km2 in the dry season to about 24,605 km2 in the rainy season, and the plain around it, devoted to wet rice cultivation, is the heartland of the country.
The highest peak is Phnom Aural, at 1,813 metres. The Khmer name derives from the Sanskrit Kambujadeśa, the land of the sons of Kambu, after a sage from whom the Khmer kings claimed descent.

Cambodia has been inhabited for over 5000 years. The cave of Laang Spean, with radiocarbon dates around 6000 BCE, is considered the most ancient archaeological site in the country, and the first rice farmers came from the north from the third millennium BCE. Iron was worked by about 500 BCE. In the 3rd, 4th and 5th centuries the Indianised kingdoms of Funan and its successor Chenla coalesced in what became Cambodia and southwestern Vietnam, and for more than 2,000 years the region absorbed influences from India and passed them to other Southeast Asian civilisations.

In 802 Jayavarman II declared himself king, uniting the warring Khmer princes of Chenla under the name Kambuja, and the Khmer Empire became the centre of power. Over 600 years it facilitated the spread of first Hinduism and then Buddhism across Southeast Asia. In the 15th century Cambodia declined and lost territory to its neighbours, and during the Post-Angkor period Vietnam and Thailand each attempted to vassalise it. It became a French protectorate in 1863 and secured independence in 1953.

The Khmer Rouge regime carried out the Cambodian genocide from 1975 to 1979 and was deposed by a Vietnamese intervention and occupation, though insurgencies continued until 1999. By 1993 a United Nations peacekeeping mission had restored the monarchy and established a democratic constitution with elections. Cambodia is a constitutional monarchy. About 17 million people live there, 95.8% of them ethnic Khmer.
cameroon: Cameroon covers 475,442 square kilometres in Central and West Africa, on the Bight of Bonny, part of the Gulf of Guinea. It is often called Africa in miniature because it has the coast, desert, mountains, rainforest and savanna of the continent. The country divides into five major geographic zones, among them a hot and humid coastal plain and the South Cameroon Plateau, covered by equatorial rainforest.

A chain of mountains, hills and plateaus, the Cameroon range, runs from Mount Cameroon on the coast, the highest point at 4,095 metres, almost to Lake Chad in the north. Volcanism there has created crater lakes. On 21 August 1986 one of them, Lake Nyos, released carbon dioxide and killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.

Excavations at Shum Laka in the Northwest Region show human occupation dating back 30,000 years. The Baka are counted among the longest continuous inhabitants, and Bantu migrations into eastern, southern and central Africa are believed to have begun from this area about 2,000 years ago. The Sao culture arose around Lake Chad about 500 CE and gave way to Kanem and its successor, the Bornu Empire, while kingdoms, fondoms and chiefdoms arose in the west. Portuguese sailors reached the coast in 1472 and named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, the Shrimp River, after the ghost shrimp they found there. In 1896 Sultan Ibrahim Njoya created the Bamum script for the Bamum language.

Germany built a warehouse on the Wouri estuary in 1868, and in 1884 the German Empire claimed the territory as the colony of Kamerun after Gustav Nachtigal made a treaty with a local king. The people resisted in the Bafut Wars and Adamawa Wars. Commercial companies ran local administration and used forced labour on banana, rubber, palm oil and cocoa plantations, a policy criticised by other colonial powers. After World War I the territory was divided between France and the United Kingdom as League of Nations mandates. The French-administered part became independent as the Republic of Cameroun in 1960 under Ahmadou Ahidjo, and the southern part of British Cameroons federated with it in 1961.

Yaoundé is the capital and Douala, the economic capital and main seaport, is among the largest cities. Cameroon is a unitary presidential republic. Its official languages are French and English, and its people speak some 250 native languages. Christianity is the majority religion, with significant minorities practising Islam and traditional faiths. Cameroon is a member of the African Union, the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
canada: Canada is the second-largest country by total area, encompassing 9,984,670 square kilometres, and has the world's longest coastline, of 243,042 kilometres. It shares the world's largest land border with the United States, spanning 8,891 kilometres. The country has seven physiographic regions, among them the Canadian Shield, the Interior Plains and the Western Cordillera. It has over 2,000,000 lakes, and boreal forests prevail throughout. Canadian Forces Station Alert, on the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, is the world's northernmost settlement.

Indigenous peoples have continuously inhabited what is now Canada for thousands of years, and they include the First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Their population at the time of the first European settlements is estimated at between 200,000 and 2 million, and it declined by 40 to 80 percent as a consequence of colonization, through European diseases, conflicts over the fur trade, conflicts with colonial authorities and settlers, and the loss of land.

British and French expeditions explored and later settled along the Atlantic coast from the 16th century, and France ceded nearly all of its colonies in North America in 1763. Early interactions were relatively peaceful, but friendship and peace treaties gave way to the dispossession of Indigenous lands.

Canada was formed in 1867 through Confederation as a federal dominion of four provinces. Settler colonialism peaked in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the government funded Indian residential schools administered by Christian churches. These are considered part of a genocide of Indigenous peoples because of their forced assimilation and the large-scale removal of children from their families. A reconciliation commission was formed in 2008. Autonomy from the United Kingdom grew through the Statute of Westminster, 1931, and the Canada Act 1982 severed the remaining legal dependence.

Canada has ten provinces and three territories, with Ottawa as the capital and Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver as the three largest metropolitan areas. It is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, and it is officially bilingual in English and French in the federal jurisdiction. The 2021 census enumerated 36,991,981 people, and the population is estimated to have passed 40,000,000 in 2023. About 80 percent live within 150 kilometres of the border with the contiguous United States. Multiculturalism is official state policy.
cape-verde: Cape Verde is a horseshoe-shaped cluster of ten volcanic islands, nine of them inhabited, and eight islets, with a land area of about 4,033 square kilometres. They lie between 600 and 850 km west of Cap-Vert on the Senegalese coast, from which the country takes its name. Cap-Vert comes from the Portuguese Cabo Verde, meaning green cape, a name Portuguese explorers gave to the headland in 1444. The islands are divided into the Barlavento or windward group in the north and the Sotavento or leeward group in the south. Santiago is the largest and holds the capital, Praia.

The islands were uninhabited before the arrival of Europeans. Genoese and Portuguese navigators found them around 1456. Portuguese records credit the first discoveries to António de Noli, born in Genoa, who was later appointed governor by King Afonso V. In 1462 Portuguese settlers founded Ribeira Grande on Santiago, today called Cidade Velha, the first permanent European settlement in the tropics.

In the 16th century the islands prospered from the Atlantic slave trade. The English privateer Francis Drake sacked Ribeira Grande twice in 1585, when it was part of the Iberian Union, and after a French attack in 1712 the town declined relative to Praia, which became the capital in 1770. The decline of the slave trade in the 19th century brought economic crisis, but the islands' position on mid-Atlantic shipping lanes made them a good place to resupply ships, and the harbour of Mindelo grew into a commercial centre. In 1951 Portugal changed the status of Cape Verde from a colony to an overseas province in an attempt to blunt nationalism. The country became independent in 1975.

Cape Verde is a unitary semi-presidential republic whose constitution was adopted in 1980 and revised in 1992, 1995 and 1999. Praia is the capital and largest city. Portuguese is the official language, and Cape Verdean Creole, called Kriolu, is the mother tongue of virtually all Cape Verdeans. The people descend from Africans, free or enslaved, and Europeans of various origins, and the diaspora outnumbers the people on the islands.
central-african-republic: The Central African Republic is a landlocked country in the interior of Africa, bordered by Cameroon, Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo. Much of it is a flat or rolling plateau savanna about 500 metres above sea level. Two-thirds of the country lies within the basin of the Ubangi River, a tributary of the Congo, and the remaining third within the basin of the Chari River, which flows into Lake Chad. About 36 per cent of the country is forest, with the densest forest in the south.

The name comes from the country's location in Central Africa and its republican government. During the colonial era it was called Ubangi-Shari, after the Ubangi and Chari rivers. Barthélemy Boganda, the first prime minister, favoured the name Central African Republic, reportedly because he envisioned a larger union of countries in Central Africa. From 1976 to 1979 the country was known as the Central African Empire.

The region has been inhabited since at least 8000 BCE. About 10,000 years ago desertification forced hunter-gatherer societies south into the Sahel, where some settled and began farming. Before 3000 BCE the domestication of the African oil palm improved nutrition and allowed populations to expand. The Bouar Megaliths in the west indicate an advanced level of habitation in the late Neolithic, c. 3500 to 2700 BCE, and ironwork developed in the region around 1000 BCE. The Ubangian people settled along the Ubangi River, and some Bantu people migrated from southwest Cameroon.

In the 16th and 17th centuries slave traders raided the region as part of the expansion of the Saharan and Nile slave routes, and captives were shipped to the Mediterranean coast, Europe, Arabia and the Western Hemisphere. In the 18th century the Bandia-Nzakara Azande peoples established the Bangassou Kingdom along the Ubangi. In the mid 19th century the Bobangi people became major slave traders. The borders were established by France, which began annexing portions to the French Congo in the late 19th century and in 1903 created the separate colony of Ubangi-Shari, part of French Equatorial Africa.

The Central African Republic became independent from France in 1960. Its capital and largest city is Bangui, on the southern border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its people belong to about 80 ethnic groups, the largest being the Gbaya and the Banda. French and Sango, a creole based on the Ngbandi language, are the official languages. The Aka of the south-west have a vocal tradition of contrapuntal polyphony in four voices.
chad: Chad is a landlocked country of 1,284,000 square kilometres, bordered by Libya, Sudan, Niger, Nigeria, Cameroon and the Central African Republic. Its capital is 1,060 kilometres from the nearest seaport, Douala in Cameroon, and the distance and desert climate have led to the nickname Dead Heart of Africa. A wide basin is bounded by the Ennedi Plateau and the Tibesti Mountains, which include the dormant volcano Emi Koussi, at 3,414 metres. Lake Chad is the remains of an immense lake of 330,000 square kilometres that existed 7,000 years ago. The Sahara covers the northern third, a Sahelian belt lies in the centre, and savanna in the south.

From the 7th millennium BCE ecological conditions favoured settlement in the north, and some of Africa's most important archaeological sites are in the Borkou-Ennedi-Tibesti Region. The earliest civilisation of the Chad Basin was the Sao, known from artefacts and oral histories, which fell to the Kanem Empire. Kanem became the first and longest-lasting of the states in the Sahelian strip, its power based on the trans-Saharan trade routes. Islamisation increased from the 11th century, and by the 12th century its scribes had developed an original script style, the barnāwī.

Kanem's expansion peaked under Mai Dunama Dabbalemi, who reigned c. 1221 to 1259. Around 1396 Bulala invaders forced Mai Umar Idrismi to move the imperial centre to Bornu. The Sultanate of Bagirmi and the Wadai Sultanate arose in the 16th and 17th centuries, and Wadai's Muhammad Sharif, who reigned from 1843 to 1858, subjugated Bagirmi and resisted French colonisation. The Territoire Militaire des Pays et Protectorats du Tchad was created in 1900, and by 1920 France had secured full control and made Chad part of French Equatorial Africa.

Chad became independent in 1960 under François Tombalbaye. Resentment of his policies in the Muslim north led to a civil war that began in 1965, and rebels took the capital in 1979. Hissène Habré defeated rival commanders, and a Chadian–Libyan conflict that began in 1978 ended in 1987 with French military intervention. Idriss Déby overthrew Habré in 1990. Chad has over 200 ethnic and linguistic groups, and its official languages are French and Arabic. Islam is practised by 55.1 per cent and Christianity by 41.1 per cent.
chagatai-khan: Chagatai was born in late 1183 or 1184 to Börte, of the Onggirat tribe, and Temüjin, the later Genghis Khan. Because Börte had been kidnapped by the Merkit tribe before the birth of her elder son Jochi, whose paternity was never known, Chagatai was the first son definitively fathered by Temüjin. When Genghis divided his new nation after the assembly of 1206, Chagatai received territories near the Altai Mountains and either 4,000 or 8,000 subjects. He was known for his knowledge of Mongol law and custom, and chroniclers such as Juzjani noted the harshness of his temperament.

With his brothers Jochi and Ögedei he commanded the right wing in the invasion of the Jin dynasty in 1211. In the invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219 he was charged with building bridges and maintaining roads. He and Ögedei besieged Otrar, which fell in February 1220; the Mongols killed or enslaved its entire population. At the Siege of Gurganj, which fell in April 1221, the usual narrative has Chagatai and Jochi quarrel over how to conduct it until Genghis placed Ögedei over both; the historian Christopher Atwood argues that this account was a later invention meant to support Ögedei's right to rule.

Genghis thought Chagatai too strict and narrow-minded for a ruler and was troubled by his hatred of Jochi, and excluded him from the succession. After Genghis died in 1227, Chagatai held to his father's will, prevented any usurpation before the accession of Ögedei in 1229, and presided over the coronation with Tolui and their uncle Temüge. In Central Asia his capital and summer pastures were at Almaliq. He disputed jurisdiction with the imperial official Mahmud Yalavach, and when Bukhara revolted against tax demands in 1238 he left its suppression to Ögedei's armies.

After Ögedei died in December 1241, Chagatai's support made Töregene regent. He died in 1242; his wife Yesülün accused a steward named Vajir of poisoning him and had him executed. His grandson Qara Hülegü succeeded him but was displaced by Chagatai's son Yesü-Möngke between 1246 and 1250.

Chagatai upheld traditional Mongol law, which forbade elements of Islamic practice, and gained a reputation for being anti-Muslim; one contemporary Muslim writer claimed that he urged Ögedei to kill every Muslim in the empire. The historians Michael Hope and Peter Jackson think this far from the truth, pointing to the powerful Muslim officials at his court. His descendants were nonetheless far slower to convert to Islam than the rulers of the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate.
chand-dynasty: The traditional genealogical lists of the Chand kings, the vamshavalis, were compiled in the mid-19th century and are not completely reliable. They place Som Chand in the 7th century, and a British report of 1849 accordingly dated the start of Chand rule to 685 CE. Historians dispute this, because the Katyuri kingdom is known to have ruled Kumaon until the third quarter of the 10th century.

Tradition makes Som Chand an immigrant from Jhusi and a relative of the king of Kannauj. The historian Krishna Pal Singh suggests that he came to Kumaon during the upheaval of the Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj in 1018–1019, and dates the beginning of Chand rule to 1019–1021. By the early 13th century the Chands appear to have ruled as feudatories: the Baleshwar Temple inscription of 1223, set up by Krachalla Deva, a conqueror from present-day Nepal, lists men whose names suggest that they belonged to the family.

Rudra Chand (1565–1597) seized Sira in 1581 and made the first of several attacks on the Garhwal Kingdom, all of which were repulsed. In 1587 he visited the Mughal emperor Akbar at Lahore as a mark of obeisance, and the Ain-e-Akbari lists a Sarkar of Kumaon. Baz Bahadur Chand (1638–78), one of the most powerful of the line, joined Shahjahan in an attack on Garhwal in 1655 that captured the Terai region including Dehradun, and extended his territory east to the Karnali river. In 1672 he began a poll tax whose revenue was sent to Delhi as tribute.

In 1744 the Rohilla leader Ali Mohammed Khan sent a force that took Almora against weak resistance. The Rohillas stayed seven months and left after a payment of three lakh rupees; a second attack was defeated at Barakheri. Hill troops under Dip Chand later fought beside the Rohillas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Internal strife over the following thirty years cost the kings most of the land they had held in the plains.

The Gurkhas invaded early in 1790, crossing the Kali River, and the Chands were driven to the Bhabhar and finally expelled. Nepalese rule lasted twenty-four years. During the Anglo-Nepalese War Harak Deo Joshi, minister of the last Chand raja, sided with the British, who captured Almora on 26 April 1815; with the Treaty of Sugauli, ratified on 4 March 1816, Kumaon passed to British rule. Champawat, the first capital, keeps a medieval fort and the Baleshwar and Nagnath temples, and Chand kings also built temples at Bageshwar, Bhimtal and Almora.
charles-darwin: Charles Robert Darwin was born on 12 February 1809 at The Mount, his family's home in Shrewsbury, Shropshire, the fifth of six children of the wealthy doctor and financier Robert Darwin and Susannah Darwin, née Wedgwood. His grandfathers Erasmus Darwin and Josiah Wedgwood were both prominent abolitionists, and Erasmus had praised general concepts of evolution and common descent in his Zoonomia (1794). His mother died in July 1817. In October 1825 he entered the University of Edinburgh Medical School, found lectures dull and surgery distressing, and neglected his studies. He assisted Robert Edmond Grant's research on marine invertebrates, then studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, from 1828 to 1831.

His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836, established him as an eminent geologist, and his observations supported Charles Lyell's concept of gradual geological change. The Voyage of the Beagle (1839) made him a popular author. Puzzled by the distribution of the wildlife and fossils he had collected, he devised his theory of natural selection in 1838, but he needed time for extensive research and his geological work had priority.

In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay outlining the same idea, which led to a joint submission to the Linnean Society of London. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, and later The Descent of Man (1871), on human evolution and sexual selection. His final book was The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881). He and his wife and cousin Emma Wedgwood had ten children, two of whom died in infancy.

Darwin died on 19 April 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey. By the 1870s the scientific community and most of the educated public accepted evolution as a fact, though many favoured explanations that gave natural selection only a minor role. A broad consensus that natural selection is the basic mechanism came with the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s to the 1950s. Later movements, among them eugenics and Social Darwinism, invoked his name, sometimes against his own comments; he insisted that social policy should not be guided simply by concepts of struggle and selection.
charles-dickens: Charles John Huffam Dickens was born on 7 February 1812 at Landport in Portsea Island (Portsmouth), the second of eight children of Elizabeth and John Dickens, a clerk in the Royal Navy Pay Office. He spent his formative years at Chatham in Kent, reading widely, including Tobias Smollett, Henry Fielding and The Arabian Nights. At 12 he left school to work in a boot-blacking factory when his father was imprisoned for debt, and after three years he returned to school.

Dickens began as a political journalist, reporting Parliamentary debates and election campaigns. His journalism in periodicals formed Sketches by Boz in 1836, Boz being a family nickname. His literary success began with the serial publication of The Pickwick Papers in 1836, and within a few years he was an international celebrity. In December 1845 he became editor of the Daily News but resigned after ten weeks.

On 9 June 1865, returning from Paris with Ellen Ternan, he was in the Staplehurst rail crash in Kent, in which ten passengers were killed. He tended the wounded until rescuers came and went back for the manuscript of Our Mutual Friend.

Dickens wrote 15 major novels, several novellas and many short stories. Most were published in weekly or monthly instalments, which became the dominant Victorian mode, and let him judge his audience's reaction and sometimes change his plot. Among his works are A Christmas Carol (1843), David Copperfield (1849 to 1850) and Bleak House (1852 to 1853), a satire on the judicial system that helped support a reformist movement leading to the legal reform of the 1870s. His works have never gone out of print.
chavundaraya: In his own writing Chavundaraya claims descent from the Brahmakshatriya line, Brahmins who had taken Kshatriya status. The 10th-century Algodu and Arani inscriptions name him as the grandson of Govindamayya and the son of Mabalayya, a subordinate of King Marasimha II; the family's political position under that king is believed to have led to its gradual adoption of Kshatriya status. He was a devotee of the Jain teachers Nemichandra and Ajitasena Bhattaraka, and a eulogy of him is inscribed on the Tyagada Brahmadeva Pillar at Shravanabelagola, whose base shows him with his guru Nemichandra.

The Western Gangas were feudatories of the Rashtrakutas, and as their commander Chavundaraya fought many battles for those overlords, beginning in the days of the Rashtrakuta king Khottiga Amoghavarsha. In the last years of Rashtrakuta rule the Gangas were threatened by civil war and by invasions of the Chola dynasty. When civil war broke out in 975 he supported Prince Rachamalla IV and installed him on the throne.

In the same year he suppressed a rebellion by Panchaldeva Mahasamanta, and in the battle of Bageyur he killed Mudurachayya, avenging the death of his own brother Nagavarma. His exploits earned him titles such as Samara Parashurama and Vira Martanda. He remained influential into the reign of Rachamalla V, who ruled from 986 to 999.

The Chavundaraya Purana, also known as the Trishashtishalaka Mahapurana, is the second oldest existing prose work in Kannada. It is based on two Sanskrit works, the Adipurana of Jinasena and the Uttarapurana of Gunabhadra, and tells the legends of sixty-three figures of Jain tradition: twenty-four tirthankaras, twelve chakravartis, nine balabhadras, nine narayanas and nine pratinarayanas. It was meant mainly for ordinary readers and avoided the complicated elements of Jain doctrine. He also wrote the Charitrasara in Sanskrit, and he patronised the Kannada grammarians Gunavarma and Nagavarma I and the poet Ranna.

The statue of Bahubali that he commissioned stands on the Indragiri hill, also called Vindhyagiri. Carved from fine-grained white granite, it is 60 feet tall, with a face measuring 6.5 feet, and has no support up to the thighs. The Chavundaraya basadi on the Chandragiri hill is credited to him by some scholars and to his son Jinadevana by others; another view holds that it was consecrated in the 11th century in his memory.
china: China covers 9.6 million square kilometres, the third largest country by area, with a dry and mountainous west and both mountains and wide river valleys in the east. Chinese civilization was traditionally centred in the lowlands around the two longest rivers, the Yangtze and the Yellow River, both of which originate on the Tibetan Plateau. Mount Everest, the world's highest point, lies on the border with Nepal. The climate is dominated by dry seasons and wet monsoons, and the Yellow River's perennial floods have devastated the surrounding plains throughout recorded history.

Modern Homo sapiens are attested in China from around 50,000 years ago, and pottery-making Neolithic cultures emerged after about 8,000 BCE. After 2000 BCE the Erlitou culture emerged in the Central Plain, controversially identified with the Xia, the traditionally accepted first dynasty; no written records confirm this. The Shang dynasty purportedly succeeded the Xia around 1600 BCE, and its late phase is attested by oracle bone script, the earliest known writing in China. The Zhou overthrew the Shang c. 1046 BCE, and centralised authority collapsed in 771 BCE. The Eastern Zhou saw the Spring and Autumn period and then the seven Warring States, and schools of thought such as Confucianism and Daoism.

In 221 BCE the Qin ruler Qin Shi Huang proclaimed himself the first emperor, but the dynasty lasted only fifteen years. It was followed by the Han dynasty, and two millennia of imperial rule across periods of unity and division followed. The empire was succeeded by the Republic of China after the 1911 Revolution. The Warlord Era and the Chinese Civil War followed, interrupted by the Second Sino-Japanese War. In 1949 the Chinese Communist Party proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan; both sides still claim political legitimacy. The party's attempts to advance its political program faltered through famine and political turmoil, and the reform and opening-up that began in 1978 moved China towards a socialist market economy.

The 2020 census recorded a population of 1,411,778,724, and Beijing is the capital. China is a unitary state with the Chinese Communist Party as its sole ruling party. It maintained a one-child policy from 1979 to 2015.

The Han are the dominant ethnicity, and 55 minorities are recognised, including the Hui, Mongols, Tibetans, Uyghurs and Zhuang. It has 60 World Heritage Sites, including the Great Wall and the Grand Canal.
chinvat-bridge: The Avestan name, Cinvatô Peretûm, is rendered as bridge of judgement or as beam-shaped bridge; other forms of the name are Chinwad, Cinvat, Chinvar and Chinavat. How the bridge appears depends on the asha, the righteousness, of the soul that comes to it. Three divinities are thought to be its guardians: Sraosha, who stands for conscience, Mithra, for covenant, and Rashnu, for justice. Believers hold that the souls that cross successfully are united with Ahura Mazda. The Yasna describes the bridge in its 71st chapter and the Vendidad in its nineteenth fargard.

The bridge has often been identified with the rainbow or with the Milky Way, as in C. P. Tiele's History of Religion. Other scholars, among them C. F. Keary and Ferdinand Justi, reject this reading, citing descriptions of the bridge as rising straight upward and not in a curve.

Cyrus Niknam, a mobad and writer on ancient Iranian culture, denies that Zoroaster taught a bridge at all. In his reading the phrase in the hymns means a passage concerned with how to live, a questioning of the conscience, with no material crossing for the soul. He holds that the priests of the Sasanian era adapted beliefs about heaven, hell and the afterlife from other cultures that had reached Iran, and that the picture of a bridge wide for the righteous and thin as a hair for sinners belongs to that later development, as does the Book of Arda Viraf, and not to the Gathas.

The most notable of the Sogdian depictions is on the east wall of the funerary couch of the sabao Wirkak, excavated at Xi'an; a fragmentary one is on the couch in the Miho Museum. As-Sirat in Islam is a similar idea. In Yazidism the Silat Bridge at Lalish leads to the holiest Yazidi shrine, marks the passage from the profane world to the sacred, and is held to play a part at the end of times as well. In modern literature Charles Olson refers to the bridge in The Maximus Poems, and Dimitris Lyacos alludes to it in With the People from the Bridge.
chutia-people: The origin of the name Chutia is not known; the chronicles written in the Ahom language called the kingdom Tiora, while those in Assamese used Chutia. The historic Chutias are thought to have had some Shan admixture, and their ruling families are estimated to have been originally matrilineal or not entirely patrilineal. They worshipped a primordial male deity and a primordial female deity, Kechaikhati, whose worship was conducted by a priestly section identified today as the Deori people. The settlement of Brahmins in the kingdom led to the Hinduisation of its rulers, and inscriptions of the late 14th century suggest that the kings then followed the Vaishnava tradition.

After the annexation the capital region became a frontier province of the Ahom kingdom under an officer called the Sadiya-khowa Gohain, and the Chutia nobles were widely dispersed in Upper Assam. Those Chutias who had not been Hinduised were initiated in the 17th century into the Ekasarana dharma under the Mayamara Satra by Aniruddhadev. After the fall of the kingdom a new Hindu lineage was constructed, tracing the Chutias to the legendary King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha.

The community divided into several groups. The Hindu Chutias were a large section. The Ahom Chutias intermarried with the Ahoms, held high offices in the Ahom administration and were mostly absorbed. The Borahi Chutias had religious rites of their own, and the Miri Chutias fled to the Miri hills and intermarried with the Mishing. According to one chronicle, the Ahom court adopted muga silk by employing a thousand producers and weavers from the Chutia community.

Most Chutias live in Upper Assam, mostly in the interior on the banks of rivers, in villages of about 60 to 140 families. They generally live in joint families headed by the father, which at times exceeded one hundred members. Their original Tibeto-Burman language has disappeared; a British colonial officer of the 19th century wrongly identified it with the Deori language, but the Deori community is not related to the Chutias ethnically or linguistically.

Their rituals have a tribal and tantric base influenced by Hinduism and Vaishnavism. Those called Kesa-ponthi accept restrictions on meat and alcohol in their rites, while the Poka-ponthi keep the older customs. The Government of India recognises the Chutias as an Other Backward Class, and there is a political movement to include them in the list of scheduled tribes.
confucius: The name Confucius is a Latinized form of the Mandarin Kǒngfūzǐ, meaning roughly Great Master Kong, coined in the late 16th century by early Jesuit missionaries to China. His family name was Kong and his given name Qiu, meaning hill or mound. His courtesy name was Zhongni, the Zhong indicating that he was the second son in his family.

It is thought that he was born on 28 September 551 BCE in Zou, in modern Qufu, Shandong. The area was formally controlled by the kings of Zhou but effectively independent under the local lords of Lu. His father Kong He, an elderly commandant of the local Lu garrison, died when Confucius was three years old, and his mother Yan Zhengzai raised him in poverty.

Traditional accounts trace the family back through the dukes of Song to the Shang dynasty, though not all modern scholars accept this descent. He was born into the class of shi, between the aristocracy and the common people, and was educated at schools for commoners. At 19 he married Qi Guanshi, and a year later their son Kong Li was born. He is said to have held various government jobs in his early 20s and to have mourned his mother for three years.

In the Analects, Confucius presents himself as a transmitter who invented nothing. He put the most emphasis on study and wanted his disciples to master older classics rather than build a systematic theory. Tradition credits him with authoring or editing the Five Classics, but modern scholars are cautious about attributing particular assertions to him, since some of the texts and philosophy associated with him are more ancient, and the Analects were compiled many years after his death. His ethics stress self-cultivation and emulation of moral exemplars over rules, and he taught a negative form of the Golden Rule, sometimes called the Silver Rule.

His disciples and his grandson Zisi continued his school, and Mencius in the 4th century BCE and Xunzi in the 3rd century BCE elaborated his ideas in different ways. The Qin state, which conquered all of China in 221 BCE, adopted Legalism as its official doctrine. Under Emperor Wu of Han, works attributed to Confucius were made the official imperial philosophy and required reading for civil service examinations in 140 BCE, a practice continued nearly unbroken until the end of imperial China in 1912.
croatia: Croatia lies on the Adriatic coast, and the sea forms its entire southwest border. It covers 56,594 square kilometres and is divided into twenty counties within four historical and cultural regions. The Dinaric Alps rise to the highest point, the Dinara peak at 1,831 metres, near the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Insular Croatia consists of over a thousand islands and islets, 48 of them permanently inhabited; the largest are Cres and Krk.

In the north the hilly Hrvatsko Zagorje and the plains of Slavonia are crossed by the Danube, Drava, Kupa and Sava. Karst topography makes up about half of the country. The area around Dubrovnik is a practical exclave, separated by land from the rest by a short coastal strip belonging to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and linked to it by the Pelješac Bridge.

The area was inhabited throughout prehistory, and Neanderthal fossils from the middle Palaeolithic were found at Krapina. Illyrians and Liburnians lived there, and the first Greek colonies were established on the islands of Hvar, Korčula and Vis. In 9 CE the territory became part of the Roman Empire. Emperor Diocletian, a native of the region, built a large palace at Split and retired there after abdicating in 305 CE. In the 5th century Julius Nepos, the last de jure Western Roman Emperor, ruled a small realm from it after fleeing Italy in 475.

Avar and Croat invasions in the late 6th and first half of the 7th century destroyed almost all Roman towns. Survivors retreated to the coast, islands and mountains, and Dubrovnik was founded by survivors from Epidaurum. The origin of the Croats is debated: the predominant view is that the White Croats were a Slavic group who migrated during the Migration Period, while the Iranian theory proposes a Sarmatian-Alanic origin, drawing on names in the Tanais Tablets. The oldest stone inscription with the full ethnonym styles Duke Branimir as Dux Cruatorvm, probably between 879 and 892.

Croatia is a unitary constitutional republic with a parliamentary system. The president is directly elected for five years, and the Sabor, a unicameral parliament, holds legislative power. Its population was an estimated 3.87 million in 2024, down from a peak of 4.7 million in 1991. The 2021 census recorded 91.6% Croats and 3.2% Serbs, and about 4 million Croats live abroad. The country has ten sites on UNESCO's World Heritage List. The necktie derives from the cravat worn by 17th-century Croatian mercenaries in France.
cuba: Cuba is an archipelago of 4,195 islands, cays and islets in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Gulf of Mexico meets the Atlantic Ocean. Key West, Florida, lies about 150 kilometres across the Straits of Florida to the north and northwest, Mexico 210 kilometres west across the Yucatán Channel, Haiti 78 kilometres to the east and Jamaica 148 kilometres to the south. The main island is 1,250 kilometres long and makes up most of the land area of 104,338 square kilometres. It consists mostly of flat to rolling plains apart from the Sierra Maestra in the southeast, whose highest point is Pico Turquino at 1,974 metres. The second-largest island is Isla de la Juventud.

Humans first settled Cuba around 6,000 years ago. The Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taíno arrived from South America about 1,700 years ago and, unlike the earlier settlers, produced pottery and practised intensive agriculture. The earliest evidence of the Taíno on Cuba dates to the 9th century. Descendants of the first settlers persisted in the west of the island until European contact as the hunter-gathering Guanahatabey. Christopher Columbus first arrived on 27 October 1492, claimed the island for Spain and named it Isla Juana after John, Prince of Asturias.

The first Spanish settlement was founded by Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar at Baracoa in 1511, and San Cristóbal de la Habana was founded in 1514 and moved to its present place in 1519, becoming the capital in 1607. The Taíno were forced to work under the encomienda system.

Within a century they suffered high mortality, primarily from Eurasian infectious diseases against which they had no immunity, aggravated by harsh colonial subjugation. In 1529 a measles outbreak killed two-thirds of the few who had survived smallpox. Cuba remained part of the Spanish Empire until the Spanish–American War of 1898, was then occupied by the United States, and became independent in 1902. The Cuban Revolution of January 1959 overthrew the government of Fulgencio Batista and established a communist government under Fidel Castro.

Havana is the capital and largest city. Cuba is a socialist republic whose constitution names the Communist Party as the leading force of society and the state. Spanish culture, West African culture and the Guanahatabey and Taíno inheritance together shape Cuban culture. Cuba's population descends primarily from Spanish settlers, sub-Saharan Africans brought through the transatlantic slave trade, and pre-Columbian peoples, chiefly the Taíno and Ciboney. Havana, Camagüey, Cienfuegos and Trinidad, with colonial centres in Baroque and Neoclassical styles, are inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
cudjoe: The name Cudjoe corresponds to the Akan day name Kojo or Kwadwo, given to a boy born on a Monday. The Leeward Maroons most likely emerged in 1690, when a Coromantee rebellion broke out on Sutton's estate in western Jamaica and most of the enslaved Africans there ran away into the mountainous interior. Cudjoe was probably the son of one of the leaders of that revolt. The oral history of the Accompong Town Maroons, as told by Milton McFarlane, holds that he was the freeborn son of Naquan, who led those who fled from the estate.

According to contemporary white enslavers, Cudjoe challenged a Madagascan for the leadership of the Leeward Maroons in 1720, and by defeating and killing him became their undisputed leader. His community was known as Cudjoe's Town, or Trelawny Town. For about half a century, until the treaties of 1739 and 1740, the Maroons operated outside direct British control.

During the First Maroon War of the 1730s the English colonial forces failed to win any significant victory over Cudjoe's Leeward Maroons. The agreement of 1739 recognised them as a semi-autonomous entity and freed their land from taxes. In the 1740s some Leeward Maroons who opposed the treaty rose in revolt, and Cudjoe crushed these risings.

Two descriptions of him survive from colonial writers. The physician R. C. Dallas, writing half a century after Cudjoe lived, claimed that he was short and stout, with a large lump of flesh on his back. The slaver Thomas Thistlewood, who met him in 1750, noted in his diary that he wore a feathered hat, with a sword at his side and a gun on his shoulder, barefoot and with "somewhat a Majestic look".

One source claims that Cudjoe died in 1744, but Edward Long and Thistlewood wrote of meeting him in the 1750s and 1760s. Long described him leading his Maroons in a martial performance at Montego Bay for Governor Sir William Lyttleton in 1764, and in the same year Thistlewood heard that he had been dead for some time. The treaty had named Accompong as his successor, but Governor Roger Hope Elletson had the Trelawny Town badge of authority given instead to a Maroon officer named Lewis, leaving Accompong authority over Accompong Town only. Cudjoe Day is celebrated in Jamaica on the first Monday in January.
cyprus: Cyprus is the third largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia. It measures 240 kilometres from end to end and 100 kilometres at its widest, and lies 75 kilometres south of Turkey. Two mountain ranges, the Troodos Mountains and the smaller Kyrenia Range, enclose the central Mesaoria plain. The highest point is Mount Olympus, at 1,952 metres, in the Troodos range. Some sources place the island in Europe and others in Western Asia, within the Levant.

Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, at about the time the island's pygmy hippopotamus and dwarf elephant became extinct. Neolithic farming communities emerged by around 8500 BCE, and the village of Khirokitia dates to approximately 6800 BCE.

From around 1650 BCE copper from the Troodos Mountains drove trade and the growth of urban settlements, and the island, identified in whole or part as Alashiya, was ruled by kings who corresponded with the pharaohs of the New Kingdom of Egypt, as the Amarna letters document. Mycenaean Greeks traded there from around 1400 BCE, and a major wave of Greek settlement is believed to have followed the collapse of Mycenaean Greece.

Later the island was contested by the Assyrians, Egyptians and Persians, and Alexander the Great seized it in 333 BCE. Ptolemaic, Roman, Arab, Lusignan and Venetian rule followed, then Ottoman dominion from 1571 to 1878. Britain administered Cyprus from 1878 under the Cyprus Convention and annexed it formally in 1914. Independence came in 1960. Intercommunal violence in 1963 and 1964 displaced more than 25,000 Turkish Cypriots into enclaves.

A coup by Greek Cypriot nationalists and elements of the Greek military junta on 15 July 1974 was followed by the Turkish invasion of 20 July, which captured the north and displaced over 150,000 Greek Cypriots and 50,000 Turkish Cypriots. A Turkish Cypriot state declared in 1983 is recognised only by Turkey. The island is divided along a United Nations buffer zone, and two British sovereign military bases, Akrotiri and Dhekelia, remain in the south.

The Republic of Cyprus, a presidential republic, joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro on 1 January 2008. Greek and Turkish Cypriots share many customs, such as the foods souvla and halloumi, but differ in religion: Greek Cypriots are traditionally Greek Orthodox and Turkish Cypriots Sunni Muslim.
czech-republic: The Czech Republic is a hilly, landlocked country of 78,871 square kilometres, bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland and Slovakia. It is traditionally divided into three lands: Bohemia in the west, Moravia in the east and Czech Silesia in the northeast. Bohemia is a basin drained by the Elbe and the Vltava, surrounded by low mountains such as the Giant Mountains, where Sněžka, at 1,603 metres, is the highest point in the country. Moravia is hilly and drained mainly by the Morava River.

Water from the country flows to three seas: the North Sea, the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea. The Czech Republic also leases the Moldauhafen, a lot in the Hamburg Docks awarded to Czechoslovakia by Article 363 of the Treaty of Versailles; the territory reverts to Germany in 2028.

The area has been inhabited since the Paleolithic, and the Venus of Dolní Věstonice, dated to approximately 29,000 to 25,000 BCE, is considered the oldest known ceramic figurine in the world. After Celtic migrations in the 3rd century BCE, Bohemia became associated with the Boii. In the 7th century the Frankish merchant Samo became ruler of Samo's Empire, the first documented Slavic state in Central Europe. Great Moravia reached its zenith in the 9th century under Svatopluk I, and was Christianized with the Byzantine mission of Cyril and Methodius, who codified Old Church Slavonic and the Glagolitic script.

The Přemyslid dynasty unified the Duchy of Bohemia in the late 9th century. In 1212 Přemysl Ottokar I obtained the Golden Bull of Sicily from the emperor, confirming his and his descendants' royal status, and the duchy was raised to a kingdom. German immigrants settled in the periphery in the 13th century, and the Mongols, in their invasion of Europe, were defensively defeated at Olomouc after raiding Moravia.

The Czech Republic is a pluralist parliamentary democracy with a bicameral parliament: the 200-member Chamber of Deputies and the 81-member Senate. From 1993 to 2012 the president was chosen by parliament, and since 2013 by direct election.

In the 2021 census 57.3% of inhabitants were Czechs and 3.4% Moravians. About 75% to 79% of residents declare no religion. The Jewish population of Bohemia and Moravia, 118,000 in 1930, was nearly annihilated in the Holocaust.
